Oh, the tunes Webb has weaved

Scooter MacMillan, Editor August 20, 2026August 19, 2026

Pianist still going strong after 40 years at Shelburne Farms Inn

Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 5:53
Instaread

You might say that Paul Webb went from squeezing the udders to tickling the ivory.

In 1986, Webb had taken a job at Shelburne Farms milking cows when a friend from his days as a University of Vermont student asked him if he’d like to play piano at the Shelburne Farms Inn.

The mansion, that had been the home of Dr. William Seward Webb and his wife, Lila Vanderbilt Webb, was built in 1887 and was renovated into the inn 100 years later.

Paul Webb, no relation to the farm’s founders and descendants, had been getting up at 3 a.m. to milk the farm’s cows when his friend, who was the director of the new inn and who knew that he played the piano, asked him if he’d like to ply his musical skills there.

So, on a Friday afternoon, right after the inn’s opening, Webb cleaned up from his milking duties at the barn and went to the mansion to play the piano. It was a one-night gig that’s lasted for 40 years.

After four decades of Friday and Saturday nights at the inn’s piano, he has no plans to retire. He says ask him again in 10 years.

Webb said the songs he usually pulls from his repertoire are predominantly jazz standards from the “Great American Songbook,” Gershwin, Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hart, Rodg­­­­ers and Hammerstein — “all those guys.”

“Any song with a good melody is what I’m interested in, whether it’s a Beatles song or a George Gershwin song,” he said.

Before the Webbs’ former home was renovated into the Shelburne Farms Inn, it had been unoccupied for a number of years.

Alec Webb, great-grandson of William and Lila Webb, grew up on the farm. He recalled for Vermont Public in 2017: “When people walked in the front door in the 1960s, you would have seen two buckets catching water dripping through the ceiling. The back of the house was gone, and I mean, really, the house and the barns came within a hair of being lost in the ‘60s and ‘70s. It was a close call.”

Now, when people walk in the front door on a Friday or Saturday, they enter the grandest of mansions. To their left they’ll hear the sound of a piano, probably playing a tune they faintly remember, maybe from their childhood, but slightly altered by Webb’s gentle improvising.

The music is coming from the library, a grand room filled with books and the soft melodies of standards, whose provenance stretches from the 1930s. Sometimes the songs they hear might even be from today, if it’s a tune with a strong melody. The chances of a rap song coming from Webb’s sessions at the keyboard are less than a snowball’s chances in h-e-double hockey sticks or south Georgia in August.

Webb has noticed that in recent years, more and more people don’t recognize the standards from the mid-20th century. Recently, a man who looked to be around 45, stopped by the piano and said, “I like that song. What’s the name?”

Webb was playing “Stardust.” Although Willie Nelson recorded an album in the late 1970s called “Stardust” that featured the 1927 Hoagy Carmichael song, an album that revived the popularity of the song on a hit record that stayed on the Billboard Country Album charts for 10 years, Webb said, he was probably born in the 1980s and probably started listening to music in the 1990s, so it was still before his time.

However much musical tastes have changed and memories have faded, there’s one song that the youngest of Shelburne Farms Inn patrons invariably know. When Webb starts playing “My Favorite Things,” if there is a young girl in the library, even as young as 4 years old, “The girl starts paying attention. She and her mother might start dancing to it,” Webb said.

Although Webb is primarily a soloist, he has released several albums of his own compositions that include other musicians. His recording work has paid dividends in a satisfying and emotional way. Over the years, Webb really admired the playing and compositions of jazz and classical pianist Keith Jarrett. His son, Gabe Jarrett, a drummer who has lived and played in Vermont for around 30 years, contributed percussion to some of Webb’s albums. Webb is clearly moved to have that connection to someone he admires so much.

After graduating from the University of Vermont in 1980 with his degree in biology and psychology, Webb worked with children with emotional disabilities. One day, he was walking with some children down Battery Street, and they walked into a store where a piano was for sale.

When someone working there heard Webb’s playing, they recommended he talk to the folks at Waterworks Restaurant. The store was selling a piano to the restaurant which was just opening. That led to a 10-year gig.

Webb is quick to insist that his playing is not a concert; he doesn’t want the focus to be on him.

“They’re not there to listen to me. I’m just background music. They walk in the door, they hear some melody they haven’t heard in years on the piano, and they say, ‘Oh, that’s nice. I remember that.’ And then they get on with their visit.”

And that’s the way he likes it: “It gives me a reason to do something I like to do. Shelburne Farms has been wonderful for me.”
